##Problem 1
```{r load-noaa}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

data("ny_noaa")

dim(ny_noaa)
glimpse(ny_noaa)
```
```{r missing-data}
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))
  )

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(everything(), ~ round(mean(is.na(.)) * 100, 2))
  )
```
The NY NOAA data set has 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. The variables are station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. Missing data are an important issue in this data set. Both maximum and minimum temperatures are missing 43.71% of the time. Snow depth is missing 22.80% of the time. Snowfall is missing 14.69% of the time and precipitation is missing 5.62% of the time. The variables station ID and date do not contain any missing data.

##Data Cleaning
```{r clean-noaa}
noaa_clean = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

glimpse(noaa_clean)
```
```{r snowfall-summary}
noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  print(n = 10)
```
The most frequent snowfall value is 0 mm because most days have no snowfall. There are many missing observations. Among positive snowfall values, 25 mm, 13 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm are common. Values of 1, 0.5, 2 and 3 inches correspond to these, respectively. This suggests that snowfall was previously measured in inches and then converted to mm.

## Average Maximum Temperature in January and July
```{r january-july-temp, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
jan_jul = noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(jan_jul, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The difference between January and July is very clear. From the plots it shows January max temperatures are between -5°C and +5°C with considerable variation. July temperatures range from 25°C to 30°C. In January 1982 there was an outlier as it was unusually cold for the month. July 1988 also has an outlier as it was relatively cool for the month.

## Temperature and Snowfall
```{r temperature-snowfall, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
library(ggridges)
library(patchwork)

snow_plot = noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 1,
    fill = "gray80",
    color = "gray40",
    bandwidth = 3.76
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

temp_plot = noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 40) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

snow_plot + temp_plot
```
Snowfall distributions tend to be similar from year to year. Smaller snowfall amounts tend to occur more frequently and larger snowfall amounts tend to occur less frequently. There appear to be multiple peaks in the distributions, possibly due to the fact that originally snowfall amounts were measured in inches and then converted to the metric system.

The hexbin plot of minimum and maximum temperatures shows a positive correlation. Most of the data is in the mid range of temperatures, and extreme high and low temperatures may be outliers or represent data quality issues.

# Problem 2
```{r load-nhanes}
nhanes_covar = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)

nhanes_accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")

dim(nhanes_covar)
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

dim(nhanes_accel)
glimpse(nhanes_accel)
```
```{r tidy-nhanes}
nhanes_tidy = nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21, !is.na(sex), !is.na(age),
         !is.na(BMI), !is.na(education)) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school",
                 "High school equivalent",
                 "More than high school")
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(nhanes_accel, by = "SEQN") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min"))
  )

dim(nhanes_tidy)
glimpse(nhanes_tidy)
```
```{r demographic-table}
demographic_table = nhanes_tidy |>
  distinct(SEQN, sex, education) |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  demographic_table,
  caption = "Number of Men and Women by Education Level"
)
```
The sample consists of 228 participants, of which 118 are men and 110 are women. The largest group comprises participants with more than a high school education. This group consists of 56 men and 59 women. The next largest group comprises participants with a high school education. This group comprises 35 men and 23 women. The numbers of men and women with a lower education than high school are equal (27 and 28).

```{r age-distribution}
age_data = nhanes_tidy |>
  distinct(SEQN, sex, age, education)

ggplot(age_data, aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
Participants with less than a high school education have a relatively older median age, about 60, as do men and women in that group. High school equivalency participants also show a difference with women having a higher median age than men. Those with more education than a high school degree show a relatively younger median age in their early to mid-40s. Differences among the education groups are generally larger than differences among women and men within groups.

```{r total-activity}
activity_total = nhanes_tidy |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(activity_total,
       aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Total activity levels decrease with age across the board for all three education groups. The fitted trend lines show women in both the high school equivalent and more than high school groups having higher total activity levels than men. For the less than high school group, the trend lines are relatively similar for both genders. There is also one atypically low total activity observation in the more than high school group.

```{r daily-activity-pattern}
activity_by_minute = nhanes_tidy |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    hour = (minute - 1) / 60
  )

ggplot(activity_by_minute,
       aes(x = (minute - 1) / 60, y = mean_MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The three educational groups show similar activity patterns over the 24-hour period. Over the course of the day, activity levels decrease in the evening. On average, women are more physically active during the day than men. Women also show greater night time activity than men, especially between 11 PM and 1 AM. Activity levels among the group with less than a high school education show a morning peak, while activity among the group with more than a high school education display more evened out activity levels during the day.

# Problem 3
```{r load-citi}
citi_jan_2020 = read_csv("data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv")
citi_jan_2024 = read_csv("data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv")
citi_july_2020 = read_csv("data/July 2020 Citi.csv")
citi_july_2024 = read_csv("data/July 2024 Citi.csv")

dim(citi_jan_2020)
dim(citi_jan_2024)
dim(citi_july_2020)
dim(citi_july_2024)

glimpse(citi_jan_2020)
glimpse(citi_jan_2024)
```
```{r merge-citi}
citi_data = bind_rows(
  citi_jan_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),
  citi_jan_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),
  citi_july_2020 |> mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),
  citi_july_2024 |> mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
)

dim(citi_data)
glimpse(citi_data)
```
```{r clean-citi}
citi_clean = citi_data |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = c(2020, 2024)),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
                 "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type)
  )

glimpse(citi_clean)
summary(citi_clean$duration)
```
The cleaned Citi Bike dataset contains 99,485 rides, 9 variables and contains 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 rides. Variables are: ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting station, ending station, membership status, year, month. The average duration of a ride is 13.93 minutes, the median is 9.84 minutes. Variables, membership status, weekday, year, bike type and month, were transformed to factors for further analysis.

```{r citi-ride-counts}
ride_counts = citi_clean |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )

knitr::kable(
  ride_counts,
  caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Status"
)
```
Citi Bike members made up the vast majority of rides in all four months. July saw more rides both years than January, showing that more rides occur during the summer months. More rides occurred in 2020 than 2024. July 2024 saw the most rides of all months, with members taking 36,262 rides, and casual users taking 10,894 rides. Given that only a subset of rides was captured, it shows that Citi Bike usage has been increasing and will likely continue to rise.

```{r popular-stations}
popular_stations = citi_clean |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July") |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  rename(
    `Starting Station` = start_station_name,
    `Number of Rides` = n
  )

knitr::kable(
  popular_stations,
  caption = "Top 5 Most Popular Starting Stations in July 2024"
)
```
In July 2024, 163 trips started from Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers. The next most popular station, University Pl & E 14 St, had 155 trips. W 21 St & 6 Ave was the third most popular station with 152 trips. The other stations in the top five had similar numbers of trips with counts from 146 to 163.

```{r median-ride-duration}
median_duration = citi_clean |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(
  median_duration,
  aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = month, group = month)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```
The plot shows that the median ride duration was longer in July than in January in both years. Ride durations were also longer in 2020 than in 2024 for both months. Ride durations in July were also longer in 2020 than in 2024. Of all the months, ride durations in July 2020 were the longest. July 2020 also shows the highest median durations on weekends with Saturday and Sunday having the longest median durations. This could indicate seasonal variations and recreational use of the service.
```{r bike-type-duration}
citi_2024 = citi_clean |>
  filter(year == "2024")

ggplot(
  citi_2024,
  aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)
) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type in 2024",
    x = "Membership Status",
    y = "Ride Duration (minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The boxplots show that, in January and July 2024, casual riders clocked longer ride times than Citi Bike members. Ride times in July are longer than in January, especially for casual riders. For casual riders, classic bikes tend to have longer median ride times than electric bikes. For members, it’s the other way around. All groups, once again, show right-skewed distributions, meaning there are long-duration outliers. These results indicate that membership status, bike type, and season are associated with differences in ride duration.
